content: The belief that completing an antibiotic course, even after symptoms have resolved, is necessary to prevent the development of antibiotic-resistant bacterial strains is widely held. This concept was further investigated by Martin J. Llewelyn, a professor of infectious diseases at Brighton and Sussex Medical School. The origins of this belief trace back to the 1940s, during the early development of antibiotics. Alexander Fleming, in his Nobel Prize speech, warned that insufficient doses of penicillin for treating streptococcal throat infections could lead to the emergence of resistant bacterial strains, which could then infect other patients. Two primary mechanisms are responsible for the development of antibiotic resistance: targeted selection and collateral selection. Targeted selection occurs when bacteria, such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis, develop resistance due to the administration of an insufficient or single antibiotic. However, this mechanism accounts for only a minority of antibiotic resistance cases. Collateral selection, on the other hand, is the more common mechanism. It occurs when antibiotics disrupt the normal bacterial flora in the body, creating an environment that allows resistant and harmful bacterial strains to thrive. Importantly, collateral selection is not influenced by the duration of antibiotic administration. The role of antibiotic course duration in the development of resistance remains underexplored. For most bacterial infections, the conventional duration of antibiotic treatment has not been rigorously compared to shorter courses in terms of efficacy or the emergence of resistant strains. For example, pyelonephritis has traditionally been treated with quinolones for two weeks. However, clinical trials have demonstrated that a 5-7 day course is equally effective. In contrast, shorter antibiotic courses for otitis media did not yield the same clinical outcomes as longer courses. Interestingly, shorter courses of antibiotics have been associated with similar or even better clinical results, including lower recurrence rates, compared to longer courses. In the case of hospital-acquired pneumonia, research suggests that shorter antibiotic courses may reduce the likelihood of developing resistant bacterial strains in the future. None of the trials reviewed have shown an association between shorter antibiotic courses and increased resistance. The author suggests that antibiotic administration should be guided by infection biomarkers, such as procalcitonin, in inpatient settings, and by patient symptoms in outpatient settings. Furthermore, the traditional message of completing the course should be reconsidered and revised. However, further research is needed to confirm these findings and refine treatment guidelines.
